prompt.brief: Design a distributed API rate limiter that enforces tenant, user, credential, IP, and endpoint quotas with predictable burst behavior, low overhead, and safe degradation.
successSignals: Define quota identity, policy precedence, token or refill semantics, burst capacity, response headers, time source, and scope inheritance.
Partition counters by policy key, isolate hot tenants and endpoints, and choose strict versus approximate enforcement for multi-region traffic.
Keep the decision path bounded and atomic; handle clock skew, retries, failover, counter loss, policy updates, and cache stampedes.
Explain fail-open or fail-closed behavior by endpoint risk, abuse resistance, observability, auditability, and degraded local limits.

functional: Decide whether a request is allowed for a tenant, user, credential, IP, endpoint, or combined policy key.
Support token-bucket, leaky-bucket, fixed-window, or sliding-window policies with explicit burst behavior.
Return remaining quota, reset time, policy identity, and a retry hint when a request is rejected.
Create, version, validate, and roll out policies without leaving counters in an ambiguous state.
Support batch decisions for bounded requests and separate administrative policy reads from the hot path.
Expose counter, policy, latency, rejection, and failover health to operators and policy owners.
nonFunctional: Keep a single decision below p99 5ms at the regional edge under normal load.
Handle 1M decisions per second and 10M active policy keys with partitioned counters.
Make each decision atomic for its key and document whether multi-region enforcement is strict or approximate.
Prevent a limiter outage from taking down healthy traffic while preserving stricter protection for abuse-sensitive endpoints.
Bound counter memory, policy propagation lag, retry work, and hot-key amplification.
scaleAssumptions: Serve 1M rate-limit decisions per second over approximately 10M active tenant, user, credential, IP, and endpoint keys.
Assume a 90:10 allow-to-reject mix, with a few public endpoints and tenants producing disproportionate hot-key traffic.
Replicate policy configuration globally, but keep the counter decision local when the product accepts bounded cross-region approximation.
Expire inactive counters and retain policy versions, decision samples, and administrative audit records separately from hot counters.

metrics.label: Decision throughput
metrics.description: Capacity assumption that drives counter shards, connection pools, and local admission control.

metrics.label: Active keys
metrics.description: Working-set estimate for counters and policy scopes, excluding expired keys.

metrics.label: Decision latency
metrics.description: Budget for the atomic counter operation and policy lookup on the regional path.

metrics.label: Policy freshness
metrics.description: Example propagation target for policy versions; high-risk changes may require a stronger barrier.

metrics.label: Enforcement error
metrics.description: Explicit bound for local multi-region approximation, measured against sampled authoritative decisions.

entities.name: RateLimitPolicy
entities.notes: Versioned rules that map an endpoint request to one or more quota dimensions and specify the enforcement and failure contract.

entities.name: CounterBucket
entities.notes: Hot mutable state updated atomically by the decision service. Its expiration prevents inactive keys from consuming unbounded memory.

entities.name: RateLimitDecision
entities.notes: The response and sampled audit record for an allow or reject decision; high-volume raw decisions are sampled or aggregated.

entities.name: PolicyVersion
entities.notes: Propagation and rollout metadata that lets a region report which rules were actually enforced.

entities.name: QuotaOverride
entities.notes: A bounded, audited exception for a subject or incident; it must not bypass global safety limits or authorization.

apis.contract: { tenantId, subject, endpoint, cost?, requestId } -> { allowed, remaining, resetAt, retryAfterMs?, policyVersion }
apis.notes: Resolve applicable policies and atomically consume the requested cost from the relevant counter buckets. Return a deterministic decision for a retried request when the product requires it.
Evaluate a bounded batch with per-key atomicity; do not claim that unrelated keys commit as one global transaction.

apis.contract: { rules, expectedVersion, effectiveAt } -> { policyId, version, rolloutStatus }
apis.notes: Validate and publish a policy with optimistic concurrency, then propagate a versioned update to regional decision services.
Return configuration and rollout freshness for operators; policy reads are not a substitute for the atomic hot-path counter.

apis.contract: { subjectKey, limit, expiresAt, reason } -> { overrideId, version }
apis.notes: Create a time-bounded, authorized exception with an audit record and a safety ceiling.

dataFlow.title: Resolve the quota identity
dataFlow.description: The gateway extracts tenant, user, credential, IP, endpoint, and request cost, normalizes them, and selects the applicable policy dimensions without trusting client-supplied identity.

dataFlow.title: Load the effective policy
dataFlow.description: The decision service reads a locally cached policy version and rejects or falls back according to endpoint risk when policy freshness is outside the allowed bound.

dataFlow.title: Atomically update counters
dataFlow.description: The service evaluates each token, refill, or window bucket in one atomic operation per key and consumes cost only when the policy allows the request.

dataFlow.title: Return an actionable decision
dataFlow.description: The response includes allowed, remaining, resetAt, retryAfter, and policy version so clients and operators can distinguish quota rejection from service failure.

dataFlow.title: Propagate, expire, and audit asynchronously
dataFlow.description: Policy versions propagate to regions, inactive counters expire, hot-key and rejection metrics aggregate, and sampled decisions feed audit without slowing every check.

architecture.title: API Rate Limiter reference architecture
architecture.summary: A regional decision service resolves versioned policy and performs an atomic counter operation on the request path. Policy distribution, counter expiration, sampled audit, and observability stay asynchronous, while fail-open or fail-closed behavior is selected by endpoint risk rather than applied globally.

layers.label: Request and policy edge
layers.description: Requests enter through an authenticated boundary that identifies the subject and applies coarse protection.

layers.label: Regional decision plane
layers.description: The decision service evaluates policy and atomically updates partitioned counters.

layers.label: Policy control plane
layers.description: Versioned policies and propagation events keep regional enforcement explainable and auditable.

layers.label: Async lifecycle and audit
layers.description: Expiration, sampling, reporting, and anomaly analysis remain off the decision path.

layers.label: Reliability operations
layers.description: Latency, drift, hot keys, rejections, and failover decisions are measurable by policy and region.

keyPaths.label: Allow or reject path
keyPaths.description: Client -> gateway -> decision service -> policy cache and counter store -> response.

keyPaths.label: Policy propagation path
keyPaths.description: Policy store -> policy stream -> regional policy cache and decision services.

keyPaths.label: Async audit path
keyPaths.description: Decision service -> audit queue -> audit workers -> monitoring for sampled decisions and drift.

components.label: API callers
components.description: Services send requests through an SDK or gateway integration and consume quota headers.

properties.traffic: Tenant, user, credential, IP, and endpoint requests

components.label: API gateway
components.description: Authenticates callers, normalizes identity, applies coarse admission limits, and forwards a bounded decision request.

properties.protection: Authentication, request cost, payload bounds, and emergency limits

components.label: Rate-limit decision service
components.description: Resolves policy dimensions, evaluates buckets, and returns an allow or reject decision with quota metadata.

properties.criticalPath: Local policy plus atomic counter operation with bounded retries

components.label: Regional policy cache
components.description: Serves the latest validated policy version locally with freshness and rollout metadata.

properties.consistency: Versioned propagation with endpoint-specific stale policy

components.label: Partitioned counter store
components.description: Performs atomic token, refill, or window updates for active quota keys with TTL expiration.

properties.accessPattern: Counter key lookup and conditional update; shard hot keys separately

components.label: Policy and audit store
components.description: Stores authorized policy versions, overrides, approvals, effective times, and rollout history.

properties.correctness: Optimistic versioning and append-only administrative audit

components.label: Policy update stream
components.description: Distributes validated policy versions and invalidations to regional caches.

properties.delivery: At least once with policy version deduplication

components.label: Decision audit queue
components.description: Buffers sampled decisions, rejection signals, and counter anomalies for asynchronous processing.

properties.delivery: Durable, sampled, and partitioned by tenant and policy

components.label: Expiry and audit workers
components.description: Expire inactive state, aggregate decisions, detect drift and abuse, and build operational reports.

properties.safety: Bounded retention, sampling, and replayable processing

components.label: Limiter reliability monitoring
components.description: Tracks decision latency, policy freshness, counter errors, hot keys, rejection rate, and fail-open events.

connections.label: API request
connections.description: A caller sends a request that needs a quota decision.

connections.label: Check quota
connections.description: The gateway passes normalized identity and request cost to the regional decision service.

connections.label: Effective policy
connections.description: The decision service reads the current validated policy version locally.

connections.label: Atomic bucket update
connections.description: The service consumes or rejects cost with an atomic operation on the quota key.

connections.label: Publish policy version
connections.description: A committed policy change becomes a versioned propagation event.

connections.label: Propagate rules
connections.description: Regional caches apply policy versions idempotently and report freshness.

connections.label: Sample decision
connections.description: High-value or sampled decisions leave the hot path for audit and analysis.

connections.description: Workers process sampled decisions, expire inactive records, and detect anomalies.

connections.label: Drift and abuse signals
connections.description: Async analysis publishes policy drift, hot keys, rejection, and retention signals.

connections.label: Decision SLOs
connections.description: The hot path emits low-cardinality latency, error, and failover metrics.

deepDives.title: Token bucket and burst semantics
points: A token bucket with capacity B and refill rate R permits controlled bursts while bounding long-term throughput; define whether cost can exceed one token.
Store lastRefillAt and remaining tokens atomically, using a monotonic server time source rather than trusting client clocks.
Return reset and retry hints derived from the actual policy, not a generic fixed delay that hides burst behavior.

deepDives.title: Policy precedence and identity
points: A request may consume tenant, user, credential, IP, and endpoint buckets. Define whether all dimensions must allow and how the tightest retry hint is selected.
Resolve identity at a trusted boundary and normalize IPv4, IPv6, forwarded headers, credentials, and endpoint templates consistently.
Separate transactional traffic from bulk or public traffic so a global policy does not create accidental cross-tenant coupling.

deepDives.title: Atomic counters and hot keys
points: The counter update must be atomic for one quota key; a read followed by a write allows races that over-admit during bursts.
A popular public endpoint or tenant can still overload its counter shard; use dedicated capacity, local admission, or hierarchical limits.
Do not add a global lock to solve hot keys; isolate the key and accept an explicitly bounded approximation when product policy allows it.

deepDives.title: Multi-region enforcement
points: A globally strict counter needs coordination and spends latency or availability budget; local counters are faster but can over-admit across regions.
Choose strict, regional, or hierarchical enforcement per policy and report the policy mode in metrics and documentation.
Clock skew and delayed replication can change window boundaries, so use server time and tolerate or compensate for bounded drift explicitly.

deepDives.title: Fail-open, fail-closed, and degraded mode
points: Fail closed for abuse-sensitive or expensive endpoints when the limiter cannot make a trustworthy decision; fail open or use a local emergency limit for low-risk reads.
Cache the last validated policy and use bounded local counters during a regional dependency failure, but expose that enforcement is degraded.
Protect the counter store itself with circuit breakers, admission control, and a separate emergency budget.

deepDives.title: Policy rollout and freshness
points: Publish immutable policy versions and apply them idempotently in each region; an effectiveAt barrier can coordinate high-risk changes.
When a cache is stale, compare policy risk and freshness against the endpoint contract instead of silently using any available rule.
Retain rollout history so an operator can explain which limit was enforced for a rejected request.

deepDives.title: Retries, response headers, and cost
points: A retry may represent a new request and should normally consume quota again; if a client retry must be idempotent, define a bounded request identity and replay window.
Return standard remaining, limit, reset, and retry-after information without exposing another tenant's quota state.
Batch decisions only within bounded limits and keep partial failures explicit rather than pretending unrelated keys share a transaction.

deepDives.title: Observability and abuse detection
points: Measure decision latency, counter errors, rejection rate, policy freshness, hot-key skew, drift, and fail-open events by region and policy.
Sample high-cardinality decisions and aggregate ordinary traffic so observability does not become a second overload source.
Keep abuse analysis asynchronous; a slow detector should not delay a safe, already-bounded decision.

tradeoffs.title: Token bucket versus sliding window
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use token bucket for efficient low-latency decisions and controlled bursts; use a sliding or fixed window when boundary semantics are easier to explain or audit.
tradeoffs.caution: Window algorithms can create boundary bursts, while token bucket requires careful refill arithmetic and atomic state.

tradeoffs.title: Centralized versus local counters
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use a regional counter store for strict local enforcement and local emergency limits for resilience; document cross-region approximation separately.
tradeoffs.caution: A globally centralized counter adds latency and can become a single failure domain; independent local counters can over-admit.

tradeoffs.title: Single-dimensional versus hierarchical quotas
tradeoffs.recommendation: Combine tenant, subject, endpoint, and IP dimensions when abuse or fairness requires it, but keep the number of atomic buckets bounded.
tradeoffs.caution: More dimensions improve isolation but increase decision cost, memory, and the difficulty of explaining which bucket rejected a request.

tradeoffs.title: Fail-open versus fail-closed
tradeoffs.recommendation: Select the failure mode per endpoint risk and offer bounded local emergency limits rather than one global policy.
tradeoffs.caution: Fail-open can expose expensive or sensitive endpoints; fail-closed can turn a limiter outage into a broad application outage.

tradeoffs.title: Exact audit versus sampled telemetry
tradeoffs.recommendation: Keep the decision response authoritative and sample or aggregate high-volume audit data, retaining full records for policy changes and exceptional events.
tradeoffs.caution: Sampling reduces storage and cost but cannot answer every historical question without a defined reconstruction limit.

commonMistakes: Updating a counter with separate read and write operations and allowing concurrent requests to over-admit.
Using client time or an unbounded sliding-window log for every key, which creates correctness and memory problems.
Treating all quota dimensions and endpoint risks as identical, then applying a single fail-open or fail-closed policy.
Ignoring hot tenants, public endpoints, and counter-shard skew because average traffic is balanced.
Propagating policy without versions or freshness, making rejected requests impossible to explain after a rollout.
Putting abuse analytics, policy compilation, or global coordination on every decision's synchronous path.

followUps.question: What happens if the counter store is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Use the endpoint's declared risk policy: fail closed for sensitive or expensive actions, or use a bounded local emergency limiter for low-risk traffic, and expose degraded enforcement.

followUps.question: How do you enforce one tenant's global limit across regions?
followUps.answer: Choose between a coordinated global counter, hierarchical regional budgets, or bounded local approximation; state the over-admission bound and its operational response explicitly.

followUps.question: How do you prevent a hot key from overloading one shard?
followUps.answer: Detect skew, allocate dedicated capacity or hierarchical local admission for that subject, and preserve a bounded policy approximation rather than introducing a global lock.

followUps.question: Does a client retry consume quota twice?
followUps.answer: Normally yes because it is another request. If product semantics require retry idempotency, carry a bounded request identity and define how replayed decisions expire.

rubric.description: The answer states decision volume, active keys, latency, burst, identity dimensions, policy freshness, and an explicit enforcement drift bound.
The answer defines policy precedence, token or window semantics, atomic counters, expiration, response headers, and retry behavior.
The answer partitions counters, isolates hot keys, bounds batch work, and explains regional versus global enforcement.
The answer handles policy rollout, stale configuration, counter failure, clock skew, fail-open or fail-closed behavior, and abuse isolation.
The answer connects metrics to quota correctness and can defend algorithm, storage, multi-region, and audit choices.
